_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: Waymo opened its San Antonio robotaxis to anyone with its app, the airport included. Its federal flood recall still lists the remedy as under development.

introduction.text: [Waymo said that from {{date:c1}} anyone with its app in San Antonio, San Diego and Tampa can hail a fully autonomous ride, with San Antonio International Airport included](c1). [The city's Director of Airports called the airport service a significant milestone in a statement Waymo published](c2), [and said locals catching an early flight now have a new way to get to and from the airport](c3).

[The same week, the remedy field on the federal recall record for Waymo's flood defect still said the remedy is under development](c10). The service opened to everyone while the permanent fix for driving into standing water was still listed as unfinished.

paragraphs.text: [On {{date:c5}} Waymo said it was taking its first public riders in Dallas, Houston, San Antonio and Orlando](c5). [It invited them from the tens of thousands of people across those four cities who had downloaded its app](c6), [and said it would open the service to everyone later in the year](c7).
[Texas Public Radio reported that the San Antonio service began in a limited area of {{number:c21}} square miles](c21).

[Texas Public Radio reported that a Waymo vehicle was swept into Salado Creek by floodwater during heavy rain on {{date:c15}}](c15). [The car had no one inside and nobody was hurt](c16). [Earlier that April another Waymo vehicle was stranded in floodwaters near McCullough Avenue and Contour Drive, the station reported](c17).

[NHTSA's recall record says the software may let a vehicle slow down and then drive into standing water on higher speed roads](c8). [It says entering a flooded road can cause a loss of vehicle control and raises the risk of a crash or injury](c9). [Texas Public Radio reported that the recall notice said the vehicle detected the flooded road and kept going at a reduced speed](c18).

[The recall covers certain 5th and 6th generation Waymo automated driving systems](c12), [and the record lists {{number:c13}} potentially affected units](c13). [Waymo LLC is the manufacturer on the campaign](c14).

sections.heading: The pause, and what changed in the meantime

paragraphs.text: [Texas Public Radio reported in May that Waymo had been operating in San Antonio that week without serving riders](c20). [The station called the flood pause the company's longest in the city to date, a period in which it reviewed its flood monitoring procedures and safety protocols](c22). [Waymo had said it would reexamine how its vehicles respond to flood prone areas and severe weather alerts before restarting service](c23). [On May 10th the station reported that Waymo was expected to resume service in San Antonio that week](c26).

[As an interim step Waymo narrowed its operations with tighter weather limits and updated its vehicle maps](c10). [It told NHTSA that every affected vehicle had received that interim update by {{date:c11}}](c11).

sections.heading: What the record doesn't say yet

paragraphs.text: [The record's remedy field, read on the reporting date, still describes the remedy as under development](c10). It does not say when a permanent fix will arrive or what it will change about how the car behaves at the edge of standing water.
[Texas Public Radio wrote that the rollout has raised broader questions about how self driving vehicles deal with emergency responders in severe weather](c24).
